between: museum-framework.md §4.5, display rules for Relationship Objects: "Alternatives are one interaction away from every bridge. Selecting a bridge shows its rivals at the same visual weight as itself, per §3.10's refusal to let layout settle a question."
and: museum-framework.md §12.3 constraint V-8: "Equal visual weight is a claim, and is only made where the evidence is equal. Two rival explanations rendered identically when their evidence differs fails §3.10." CLAUDE.md standing constraints, no false equivalence: "A contested claim and an established one do not get parallel presentation."
what_disagrees: Whether rival explanations are rendered at equal visual weight. §4.5 requires equal weight for a bridge's alternatives; V-8 forbids equal weight wherever the evidence is unequal. Both cite §3.10 as their authority.
measured: Not a measurement. Both passages read in full in 13-PRODUCT-ARCHITECTURE/museum-framework.md as committed on main: §4.5 display rules, and §12.3 constraint V-8.
severity: MEDIUM - it does not affect any evidentiary claim, but it governs how rival explanations are displayed, which is where false equivalence enters a product
resolvable_here: PARTLY. The two rules can be reconciled by scope, and experience-object-model.md §9.7 does so for the Challenge object: reachability is equal for every rival, weight follows evidence. Whether that reconciliation is what museum-framework.md §4.5 intended is the framework author's to say.
effect: experience-object-model.md §9.7 (Challenge rivals) is written against V-8 and CLAUDE.md rather than against §4.5 generalised, and says so at the point of use. An earlier draft of §9.7 asserted that the two rules were not in conflict and cited only §4.5; that was a preferred-counter-narrative failure and is logged as BF-022.
action: Referred to the museum framework for a scope note on §4.5 saying whether it is confined to a bridge and its alternatives. No register row is promoted or demoted by this. Queued in 04-AUDITS/REAUDIT-QUEUE.csv as RA-021.

between: museum-framework.md §4.4, the seven domains over which a relationship is a bridge and over which transitive closure is disabled: language, ancestry, culture, artifact, religion, polity, modern identity.

"Environment" is not in the §4.4 enum, so an environment→culture bridge_type cannot be constructed, and M-6's transitive-closure rule - defined over domain boundaries - cannot be evaluated for slots 1, 4 or 6 at all.

severity: MEDIUM. It does not affect any evidentiary claim, and it does not weaken M-6 in the direction that matters - an unevaluable link is treated as unevaluable, not as permitted. It does mean the strongest anti-continuity rule in the framework has a gap in coverage precisely where an environmental thread runs.
resolvable_here: NO. The slippage originates in the framework, at §10.2 constraint 2, and extending §4.4's domain enum is the framework author's call. A specification that widened it on its own authority would be doing the thing this document spends §5 arguing against.

action: Referred to the museum framework: either environment is an eighth domain, or §10.2 constraint 2 is restated in terms of the seven. Queued alongside RA-021 as a framework-level question this repository has now raised twice from a specification.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html: 'a Harappan colony sat at Shortughai in Afghanistan, near the lapis-lazuli mines, working the blue stone for export'
and: melakeela/site MELUHHA_TO_KEEZHADI_synthesis.md section 12.8: 'Lapis lazuli mined at a Harappan colony at Shortugai (modern Badakhshan, northern Afghanistan), transported to Lothal in Gujarat and shipped from there to Oman, Bahrain and Sumer'
what_disagrees: The platform states two different things about the same site. The page says the colony WORKED the stone; the synthesis says the lapis was MINED there. Mining and lapidary working are different activities at different places - Sar-i Sang is a mine, Shortugai is a settlement - and the synthesis additionally routes the material through Lothal to the Gulf, which the page does not. Both are stated in the declarative. Both cite sources marked 'source listed, not accessed'.
measured: Yes - the two texts were read and compared. Neither claim could be checked against any source, because nothing on Shortugai is retrievable in this session (DR-NEG-002).
severity: HIGH. Shortugai is the load-bearing site of THE BLUE ROAD on this platform: it is what makes the Indus a participant in the lapis trade rather than a recipient of it.
effect: Three claims are packed into the page's sentence - that there was a Harappan colony, that it was near the mines, and that it worked lapis for export - and a fourth into the synthesis, that the lapis was mined there. Each is separately evidenced or not, and at present none is evidenced here. Under the ten-field discipline 'mined at' is a geological-source claim, 'working for export' is a workshop and exporter claim, and 'transported to Lothal' is an intermediary claim.
action: Do not correct either text from memory - the site is well known, which is exactly the condition under which an unretrieved recollection enters a page as a fix (BF-031). Reconcile the two statements once HOLD-008 clears, and until then mark the Shortugai sentences on both as resting on an unaccessed source.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html: 'A Sumerian scribe recording "interpreter of Meluhha" is documenting, from the outside, that the Indus people spoke a distinct language of their own'
and: This unit's corpus measurement (DRM-026) and bridge test BR-R-003
what_disagrees: The page draws a language conclusion about a population from a single administrative title. Three steps are compressed: that the title's Meluhha is the Indus, that the people so designated are the people of the Indus cities, and that the language interpreted was theirs. The corpus shows the title eme-bal / eme-bala 25 times, attested with Marhashi, Martu and Gutium and not once with Meluhha, so employing interpreters for eastern and northern neighbours was ordinary administrative practice and the Meluhha instance is not remarkable in kind. It also shows that individuals designated dumu me-luh-ha in Ur III Girsu bear Sumerian theophoric names.
measured: Yes. 25 occurrences of the title located and classified; the Meluhha instance not present in the corpus searched and typed at DR-NEG-013 as a corpus-coverage absence, not an absence in the record.
severity: MEDIUM-HIGH. The inference is reasonable in its weak form - an interpreter implies a language barrier - and the page states it in a strong form the evidence does not reach. The page's own limits section is more careful than its body, which is where the inconsistency actually lies.
resolvable_here: PARTLY. The corpus work is done; the seal inscription itself is not retrieved (HOLD-011).
effect: The defensible statement is that a Mesopotamian institution recorded a paid interpreter for people it called Meluhhan, which attests a language barrier between that institution and those people. It does not attest what language they spoke, whether it was one language, or that it was the language of the Indus cities. This platform already argues elsewhere that names record the namer's frame of reference; the same discipline applies here.
action: Weaken the body text to match the page's own limits section, and add the Marhashi, Martu and Gutium comparanda, which make the point better: the practice was general, and the Meluhha case is one object.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html: 'There is no Indus text naming Ur, Akkad, Dilmun, or anywhere at all'
what_disagrees: A negative claim stated as a fact, without a typed absence. The page's own next clause supplies the reason it cannot be known - the script is undeciphered - but the sentence before it asserts the negative outright. If the script cannot be read, an Indus text naming Ur could be in a museum case and would not be recognised as one.
measured: No measurement needed; this is a reading of the page against the standard.
severity: MEDIUM. The rhetorical force of the page's strongest section rests on it.
effect: The absence type is NOT RECOGNISED, not NOT PRODUCED and not ABSENT DESPITE ADEQUATE SEARCH. The correct statement is that no Indus inscription has been READ as naming any place, which is a fact about decipherment and not about the Indus.
action: Reword to the recognition form. It costs the page nothing: 'we cannot read one' is as striking as 'there is not one' and it is true.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html citation: 'Mukhopadhyay (2023), Humanities and Social Sciences Communications ... doi:10.1089/acm.2021.0083'
what_disagrees: The DOI does not belong to the cited journal. Prefix 10.1089 is Mary Ann Liebert, Inc., and the suffix pattern acm.2021.0083 is that publisher's Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications is published by Springer Nature. The citation and the identifier point at two different things, and the identifier is the one a reader would follow.

severity: MEDIUM. The cited argument - that the Indus script ran a trade bureaucracy - is load-bearing on the page and is labelled there as 'a leading structural argument', so a reader who wants to check it is sent to the wrong object.
resolvable_here: PARTLY. The mismatch is established; the correct DOI is not, because it cannot be looked up from here.
effect: One citation on one page. It does not affect any claim in this repository, which does not use the Mukhopadhyay argument.
action: Replace the DOI with the correct one, or remove it and keep the journal, volume and year. Recorded here rather than fixed because CLAUDE.md forbids writing site code from this repository.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html: 'Marhashi (the Halil Rud in southeast Iran)' and 'Dilmun (Bahrain and Failaka), Magan (the Oman peninsula and the Iran/Makran coast)'
what_disagrees: The page carries all four toponym identifications as settled parentheses. So does the current specialist literature (DRM-024, DEP-029), so the page is not out of step with the field. But this repository could not retrieve a source for the Marhashi identification at all, and holds it at HOLD-009.
measured: Yes - seven papers in this unit state or assume the equations and none argues for any of them.
severity: LOW as a contradiction, MEDIUM as a standing exposure.
effect: Not an error on the page. It is an inherited warrant: the platform is as well founded on this as the literature is, and the literature's foundation is a handful of upstream authorities cited in a parenthesis. The page's honesty about Meluhha - it says explicitly that the identification is an inference and not certain - is not extended to the other three, and Marhashi is the one with the least support here.
action: Extend the page's existing 'honest limits' treatment of Meluhha to Marhashi, which is the weakest of the four in this repository's evidence.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html: 'Indus seals were found at Susa, Ur and other Mesopotamian sites'
what_disagrees: Two site lists for the same phenomenon do not match. The page names Susa and Ur. The source retrieved here itemises seven classic square Indus seals west of the Harappan sphere - Kish 2, Nippur 1, Girsu 2, Mesopotamia unspecified 1, Ras al-Junayz 1 - and names neither Susa nor Ur.
measured: Yes, against SRC-114's figure 14 caption, which gives the finds with references.
severity: MEDIUM, and probably definitional rather than factual.
effect: The likely explanation is that the two are counting different things: SRC-114 counts CLASSIC SQUARE seals of Indus type, while Susa and Ur have yielded Indus-related and Indus-style glyptic more broadly, including round Gulf Type seals and seals with Indus signs. If so, both statements are true of different categories and neither is wrong. That cannot be settled here. What can be said is that the quantity is small and the specialist description is 'remarkably faint', which the page's 'a trail of Indus goods heading west' does not convey.
action: Establish which category the page means and give the count. Seven of one class after a century and a half of excavation is a more interesting fact than an unnumbered trail, and it is checkable.

between: melakeela/site meluhha-trade.html timeline: '1st millennium BCE — Meluhha = Nubia. In Neo-Assyrian texts the name is applied to Kush and the Egyptian south'
what_disagrees: No disagreement on the substance, and the corpus measurement independently supports the page's structural point in a way the page does not yet use. This unit measured the shift the page describes: 20 third-millennium and Old Babylonian occurrences with the place determinative {ki} in granary and personnel records at Girsu, against 67 Neo-Assyrian occurrences with the land determinative {kur} in royal itineraries and titulature at Nineveh, with no overlap in either direction.
severity: NONE as a contradiction. Recorded as a supportable extension, and as one caution.
effect: The caution: this repository does not state the Nubia identification, because it could not retrieve a source for it (HOLD-009). The page states it and is very likely right; the platform and the register are simply at different evidentiary standings on the same proposition, and the register's silence must not be read as doubt.
action: The determinative shift is a better piece of evidence for the page's own argument than anything currently on it, and it is a measurement with P-numbers behind it. Offer it. Keep the Nubia identification sourced independently, since this repository cannot yet supply it.
